place.en: Foot of Mount Meng · Shi'ao village

_weather: 「头天夜里下过一场雨……一直下到五更天」, then 「那天一直阴着，阴到了傍晚」: the rain is over before the scene opens; the day is overcast

setup.zh: 蒙山脚下的石坳村，十七户人家，一户打猎——你家。屋顶漏雨，一场雨接满十七个盆；山，是马家的。
setup.en: Shi'ao Village at the foot of Mount Meng: seventeen households, one of them hunters — yours. The roof leaks: one night's rain fills seventeen basins. The mountain belongs to the Mas.

recap.zh: 石坳村，猎户家的孩子：爹老实，娘心细，山是马家的。
recap.en: Shi'ao village, a hunter's child: an honest father, a clever mother, and a mountain that belongs to the Mas.

zh: 十七户人家，十六户种地，一户打猎。
一下雨，屋里摆开十七个盆。
en: Shi'ao Village, at the foot of Mount Meng.
Seventeen households: sixteen farm, one hunts.
When it rains, seventeen basins come out indoors.

story.zh:
早年间——人出门靠两条腿，夜里点一盏油灯，交租交的是鹿皮和粮食——蒙山脚下流传着一个传说。传说有这么一个少年，他的人生究竟惨到什么地步？镇上的说书先生讲起他的故事来，讲不到一半，自己先哭了，哭得收也收不住，只好把听众的茶钱一文一文地退了回去。

打那以后，说书先生再也不肯讲这个故事，倒不是不忍心，实在是赔不起。

这个少年，姓沈，名小满，这一年十二岁，生得精瘦，一双眼睛黑亮黑亮的，家住蒙山脚下石坳村。若问他是做什么的，是猎户家的独子；若问他有什么特长，只有一样：饿。一年到头，他的肚子没有一天不在叫唤。

这一年秋天，他家墙上那张弓，眼看便要姓马了。

那天一早，小满是给盆吵醒的。头天夜里下过一场雨，下得不大，却下得很有耐心，一直下到五更天。
story.en:
In the old days — when people went out on their own two legs, lit an oil lamp at night, and paid their rent in deer hides and grain — a story went round at the foot of Mount Meng. It was about a boy. How bad was his life, exactly? When the storyteller in town told it, he never got halfway before he started crying himself, and cried so hard he couldn't stop, and in the end he had to hand his listeners back their tea money, one coin at a time.

After that the storyteller would never tell it again. Not because he couldn't bear to. He simply couldn't afford to.

The boy was called Shen Xiaoman. He was twelve that year, thin as a rake, with a pair of eyes black and bright as wet stones, and he lived in Shi'ao Village at the foot of Mount Meng. Ask what he did, and he was the only son of a hunter's family. Ask what he was good at, and there was just the one thing: being hungry. There wasn't a day in the year his stomach didn't growl.

That autumn, the bow on his family's wall was about to change its name to Ma.

That morning Xiaoman was woken by basins. It had rained in the night, not hard, but with great patience, right through to the fifth watch.

story_after.zh:
他娘已经在挨个儿倒盆了。她是个瘦小的妇人，头发挽得一丝不乱，身上的补丁一块挨一块，都补得方方正正。她倒一个，数一个：「一、二、三……」数到灶台底下那个，是「九」；数到他爹炕头那个，是「十三」；数到挂兽皮那间屋的门槛里头，是「十七」。十七个盆，一个不少。

他娘直起腰来，望着墙角那半缸雨水，道：「接了半缸。够洗三回衣裳，省两趟挑水。这场雨，不算白下。」

石坳村统共十七户人家，十六户种地，一户打猎，打猎的那一户便是沈家。村里人提起沈家，都要竖起大拇指，赞一声：「猎户家，那是祖传的手艺。」赞完了，再把大拇指慢慢收回去，补上一句：「祖传的穷。」

沈家两间房，一间住人，一间挂兽皮，到得下雨天，两间都住水。小满的娘说，咱家这屋顶是蒙山最有学问的屋顶，它知道雨从哪来，还知道雨往哪去。小满的爹说，这叫**天人合一**。他娘说：「你再合一次试试。」

他爹便不说话了。

这人最懂得什么时候不说话，这是他一辈子最大的本事，也是唯一的本事——哦不，还有一样，是他的左膝盖。

他爹是个黑瘦的高个子，背有点驼，站着像一张拉久了、松不回去的弓。这左膝盖，年轻时给野猪顶过一回，从此阴天疼，下雨疼，刮风疼，马家来收租之前，也疼，比村口那面铜锣还准。

那天一早，它便疼个不停，他爹揉一下，皱一下眉。他娘瞧了他一眼，问道：「它今儿说什么了？」他爹认认真真地想了一想，老老实实地道：「它说……今儿怕是有客。」

他娘便不作声了。

蒙山是马家的，至少马家自己是这么说的。原来马家老爷在县衙里有个做书吏的远房表侄，于是一夜之间，满山的树都姓了马，满山的兔子也姓了马，连满山的泉水都跟着姓了马。村里人砍一担柴，得交马家一捆；沈家打着的野物，一半归马家：打两只兔子，交一只；打一只獐子，交半扇。

有一年小满他爹喝了二两酒，壮起胆子，小声问了一句：「那山上的风，也姓马吗？」第二天，马家便开始收「山风钱」了。从那以后，他爹再也不喝酒了。

沈家一年到头，最常来的客只有一位，这位客从不空手来——手里总拎着那根短棍；也从不空手走。

喝过一碗稀得照得见人影的野菜粥，他娘把柴刀递给小满，道：「上东坡砍一担柴。早去早回。」小满出门的时候，隔壁的[阿禾]{注=ahe}正蹲在菜地里，守着一颗白菜。她梳着两根黄毛小辫，一张小脸绷得紧紧的，比那颗白菜裹得还紧。

那颗白菜是她家菜地里最大的一颗，青里透白，裹得紧紧实实，个头比阿禾的脑袋还大上一圈。一只芦花鸡刚从篱笆缝里探过头来，她手里竹竿一点，那鸡便缩了回去，手法之熟练，一看便知是守了一整个秋天的。

小满隔着篱笆道：「阿禾，守白菜呢？」阿禾头也不抬，道：「这颗白菜，我种了八十一天。我浇了一百六十二瓢水，捉了三十一条虫，撵了四十回鸡——今天这一回不算，还没撵完。我家坡田今年又少收了两成，我爹说，土一年比一年薄了。这一颗，是过冬的。」

小满道：「我上东坡砍柴，你去不去？」阿禾道：「我娘不让我出村口。」小满道：「东坡又不在村外头。」阿禾道：「上东坡要过老槐树，老槐树就是村口。」小满想了一想，竟驳她不倒。

他正要走，阿禾在身后叫住了他：「还有。你欠我半个鸡蛋。」小满一愣：「什么时候的事？」阿禾道：「上个月十五，你帮我家撵鸡，把芦花鸡撵上了房。它那天没下蛋。」小满道：「它也不是天天都下。」阿禾道：「所以只算你半个。」

小满道：「……你连个本子都没有，这种账你也记得住？」阿禾拿指头点了点自己的脑门，道：「记在这儿。」小满道：「那你要是哪天忘了呢？」阿禾面无表情地道：「我忘了，你也得还。」

东坡上的柴，早给村里人砍得稀稀拉拉。小满爬到半坡往对面看，隔着一道山谷，半山腰上一片白墙黑瓦，三进的大院子，那便是马家了。马家的屋顶，隔着一道山谷也瞧得出是不漏的，它用不着知道雨从哪里来，小满心想，它大概是蒙山最没学问的屋顶。

马家大门口有一团圆滚滚的东西在挪动，隔得太远，他瞧不真切，也不知是马家的哪位少爷，还是马家的一扇磨盘。

他砍了一担柴挑回家，坐在院子里劈，劈一根，望一眼天。那天一直阴着，阴到了傍晚，西边的云才裂开一道缝，漏出一线夕阳来。屋里头，他爹的左膝盖「咯」地响了一声。
story_after.en:
His mother was already emptying the basins one by one. She was a small, thin woman, her hair pinned up without a strand out of place, her clothes patch upon patch, every patch sewn dead square. She emptied one, she counted one: "One, two, three…" The one under the stove was "nine"; the one at the head of his father's bed was "thirteen"; the one just inside the doorway of the room where they hung the hides was "seventeen". Seventeen basins, not one missing.

His mother straightened her back, looked at the half-vat of rainwater in the corner, and said, "Half a vat. Enough for three washes, and two trips to the well saved. That rain wasn't for nothing."

Shi'ao Village had seventeen households in all. Sixteen farmed and one hunted, and the one that hunted was the Shens. When the villagers talked about the Shens they always put up a thumb and said, "The hunter's family — that's a craft handed down from father to son." Then they slowly took the thumb back and added: "Along with the poverty."

The Shens had two rooms, one for people and one for hides, and on rainy days both of them were for water. Xiaoman's mother said their roof was the most learned roof on Mount Meng: it knew where the rain came from, and it knew where the rain was going. Xiaoman's father said this was what they called **Heaven and Man as One**. His mother said, "Try being one with it once more."

His father said nothing.

The man knew better than anyone when to say nothing. It was the greatest skill he had in all his life, and the only one — oh, no, there was one more: his left knee.

His father was tall, dark and lean, and a little stooped; standing, he looked like a bow that had been drawn too long and couldn't spring back. When he was young a wild boar had gored that left knee, and ever since it ached on cloudy days, ached when it rained, ached when the wind blew, and ached before the Ma family came for the rent — more reliable than the brass gong at the village gate.

That morning it wouldn't stop aching. His father rubbed it, frowned, rubbed it again. His mother gave him a look and asked, "What's it saying today?" His father thought it over very seriously and said, honestly, "It says… we might have company today."

His mother said nothing more.

Mount Meng belonged to the Ma family — or so the Ma family said. It turned out old Master Ma had a distant nephew who was a clerk at the county yamen, and so overnight every tree on the mountain was named Ma, every rabbit on the mountain was named Ma, and even every spring on the mountain was named Ma too. If a villager cut a load of firewood, one bundle went to the Mas; of whatever game the Shens took, half went to the Mas: two rabbits, hand over one; one river deer, hand over half a side.

One year Xiaoman's father drank two ounces of wine, screwed up his courage, and asked in a small voice, "And the wind on the mountain — is that named Ma as well?" The next day the Ma family started collecting "mountain wind money". He never drank again.

All year round the Shens had one regular guest, and this guest never came empty-handed — he always carried that short club — and never left empty-handed either.

After a bowl of wild-greens gruel so thin you could see your face in it, his mother handed Xiaoman the woodcutter's knife and said, "Go up East Slope and cut a load of firewood. Go early, come back early." As Xiaoman went out, [Ahe]{注=ahe} from next door was squatting in her vegetable plot, guarding a cabbage. She wore two little yellow-haired plaits, and her small face was wrapped tighter than the cabbage.

It was the biggest cabbage in her family's plot, green shading into white, packed firm and tight, a good size bigger than Ahe's own head. A speckled hen had just poked its head through a gap in the fence; a flick of her bamboo pole and the hen pulled back again, so neatly done you could tell at a glance she'd been guarding it all autumn.

Xiaoman said across the fence, "Ahe, guarding the cabbage?" Ahe didn't look up. "I've been growing this cabbage for eighty-one days. I've poured a hundred and sixty-two ladles of water on it, picked off thirty-one grubs, and chased off the hen forty times — this time doesn't count, I'm not done chasing. Our hill field brought in two-tenths less again this year. Pa says the soil's thinner every year. This one is for the winter."

Xiaoman said, "I'm going up East Slope for firewood. Coming?" Ahe said, "Ma won't let me past the village gate." Xiaoman said, "East Slope isn't outside the village." Ahe said, "To get up East Slope you pass the old locust tree, and the old locust tree is the village gate." Xiaoman thought about it and couldn't find a way round that.

He was just about to go when Ahe called after him: "One more thing. You owe me half an egg." Xiaoman stopped. "Since when?" Ahe said, "The fifteenth of last month. You helped chase our hens and you chased the speckled one up onto the roof. She didn't lay that day." Xiaoman said, "She doesn't lay every day anyway." Ahe said, "That's why it's only half."

Xiaoman said, "…You don't even have a book. How do you remember a debt like that?" Ahe tapped her forehead with one finger. "It's written here." Xiaoman said, "And if one day you forget?" Ahe said, without any expression at all, "If I forget, you still pay."

The firewood on East Slope had long since been cut thin by the villagers. Halfway up, Xiaoman looked across: on the far side of a valley, halfway up the mountain, stood a spread of white walls and black tiles, a big house three courtyards deep. That was the Ma place. Even from across a valley you could see the Ma roof didn't leak. It had no need to know where the rain came from, Xiaoman thought; it was probably the least learned roof on Mount Meng.

Something round was moving at the Ma gate. It was too far off to make out — whether it was one of the young Ma masters or one of the Ma millstones, he couldn't tell.

He cut a load of firewood, carried it home on his shoulder pole, and sat in the yard splitting it: split one, look at the sky. It stayed grey all day, until towards evening the clouds in the west cracked open and let out a thread of sunset. Indoors, his father's left knee gave a *click*.
